claims.paraphrase: Page title.
The author's client organizations moved from WordPress to static generators fronted by a git-backed editor.
The author found the earlier CMS hard to manage and to design in, with plugins that resisted integration.
Casual editors found the earlier CMS's block editor confusing.
Static generators paired with a git-based editor were easier to work with, but non-technical editing stayed unsolved.
The organizations' users needed one integrated place for nearly all work beyond basic productivity.
Basic office productivity tools are normally supplied by Google or Microsoft suites.
The author wanted a technical side that could be left alone, which is why Cloudflare.
Cost mattered underneath both needs, since a small organization often has little to spend.
Section heading.
cairn is both an editor-oriented git-backed CMS and a SvelteKit toolkit developers build on.
By default cairn itself acts as the identity provider for the site's editors.
By default an editor signs in via a mailed link, needing neither a GitHub account nor a password.
Behind Cloudflare Access an editor can sign in through the site's own identity gate instead of the emailed link.
An Access-gated site can offer the organization's Google or Microsoft accounts for sign-in.
Link to the organization sign-in recipe.
An editor writes in a markdown editor whose live preview renders through the same function the public site uses.
A save holds the edit on a per-entry branch.
A deliberate publish copies the held edit onto main, crediting the editor as the commit author.
After publish the site deploys the way any push to its repository already does.
None of the plumbing reaches the editor.
The setup command creates the GitHub App, the repository, and the Cloudflare bindings, then deploys, in one run.
The setup command narrates its work throughout.
Setting up a git-backed CMS by hand means wiring OAuth, a repository, and hosting yourself.
The tool reduces setup to a few questions instead of a checklist of accounts.
A developer's custom screen lives inside the same admin, reusing cairn's components and its login.
Added screens read as one product, not a second app beside the CMS.
Section heading.
cairn commits fully to SvelteKit and Cloudflare, with no layer trying to hide either.
The same no-hiding-layer commitment is claimed for GitHub.
Every production cairn site the author runs is hosted on Cloudflare.
Cloudflare is preferred for its security-oriented defaults and a free tier that holds up at small-site traffic.
SvelteKit is a framework a fixed CMS can commit to and gain real leverage from.
SvelteKit offers full server rendering and first-class TypeScript.
Islands build directly on the component model, with no adapter layer over it.
A small organization's content belongs in GitHub even when nobody there has used git.
Every publish becomes a commit.
Git itself supplies the change history, the credit, and the means to roll back.
Using git spares cairn from building and running a content database of its own.
None of the three platform choices can be reversed one at a time.
cairn has no abstraction layer for swapping Cloudflare for another host later.
GitHub is the default and only repository provider the tool wires up; a developer can implement BackendProvider for another store.
Link to the backend-provider recipe section.
Adopting cairn ties a site to Cloudflare, and to GitHub too unless a developer writes the backend seam.
Section heading.
cairn is pre-1.0 and an Extension-tier seam has already moved across two minor releases.
Until 1.0 an upgrade should be verified against the site's own code, not just installed.
The migration notes are the per-version record of changes.
cairn suits a small editorial group that coordinates closely; big or anonymous contributor pools fall outside the default design.
The default identity model expects a handful of editors at most, acquainted with each other.
The zero-config identity model has two roles, owner and editor.
Scaling past a small team, with more roles or a wider contributor pool, is developer work on the auth seams.
Link to the second-audience recipe.
Without developer help, an editor can author and release entries, and also curate images and the tag vocabulary.
A developer is needed to define a new content type, build a custom screen, or change role permissions.
An organization with no developer, and no plan for one, should weigh that before starting.
Link to the admin track's list of what needs a developer.
cairn is a content manager plus admin toolkit rather than a platform, and deliberately limits itself to content and the admin frame.
Member signups, rosters, event registration, and other organization-specific features are developer code on cairn's seams, not shipped.
Building a general feature for every organization's need would bloat the engine and slow everyone who builds on it.
Even automated setup requires accounts on GitHub and Cloudflare, with the paid Cloudflare tier active from the initial deploy.
A domain purchase may be needed once a second person has to sign in.
With the tool driving, setup is manageable, yet still involves several steps rather than one sign-up.
Links to the cost picture and the second-editor requirements.
Adopting git-backed content is a commitment in its own right.
Each publish is recorded as a commit.
Git itself supplies the change history, the credit, and the means to roll back.
The organization needs a GitHub account to reach its content repository, though editors never touch it.
An organization that avoids GitHub entirely should name that friction before starting.
Section heading.
For an admin setup with no code, the admin track suffices; the extend track is for developers going further.
An editor on an already-configured site starts at the editors welcome page.
